layers.note: The subalpine forest's tree: in clumps in the parkland above the closed forest, and as krummholz near tree line.

moisture.note: Moist, well-drained ground; not in standing water.

heat_load.note: Cool aspects and snowy hollows more than hot slopes.

elevation_m.note: About 1,000 to 2,100 m in the Washington Cascades, higher in the Rockies; the limits are loose.

shade_tolerance.note: Shade tolerant: regenerates under its own canopy and under mountain hemlock.

coldest_c.note: Across its range, coldest-month means from about −18 to 0 °C; gone below −25 °C and above 4 °C.

hard_freeze_c.note: Across its range, lows to about −42 °C borne, gone where the year's coldest night falls below about −50 °C.

warmest_c.note: Across its range, warmest-month means from about 8 to 16 °C; gone below 6 °C, where summers are too short, and above 20 °C.

degree_days_0.note: About 800 to 2,800 degree-days above 0 °C, none below 500.

degree_days_5.note: About 250 to 1,400 degree-days above 5 °C, none below 100.

moisture_index.note: A moisture index from about 0.45, gone by 0.3.

summer_rain.note: No lower limit: summer-dry Cascade summers suit it; up to about 0.6 of the year's precipitation in summer, gone by 0.8.

provenance.notes: Authored for the Mount Rainier subalpine meadow scene (Paradise, about 1,650 m) from general knowledge of the species; not yet checked against the public-domain USDA references (Silvics of North America, the Fire Effects Information System, PLANTS). Subalpine fir grows from Yukon to Arizona and New Mexico, at tree line in the Cascades and the Rockies (Silvics of North America). Each climate range brackets the climate of that range, an approximate envelope read from these descriptions, not fitted to occurrence records.
